children.value: One night, given to God: worship, prayer, beauty and practical love offered without asking anyone to surrender their conscience.
Perth Encounter is a night of prayer, worship, lament, reconciliation and practical mercy beside the Derbarl Yerrigan / Swan River.
It grew from one person’s search for God, truth, love and responsible power. It is now offered beyond one person: to Perth’s churches, communities, musicians and neighbours as one night given to God.

Its kenotic centre is simple: power is most trustworthy when it serves rather than dominates. We take revelation seriously without turning testimony into control, and we make room for doubt, conscience and honest disagreement.
“The power of revival is not how many people fall down, but how many burdens are lifted when we stand.”
The event is the visible summit of a larger offering: a humane architecture for worship, discernment, cooperation and repair.
Aaron’s account, the wider story and the questions that remain open.
Open tools for churches and communities to keep generating good work.

Silence, consent, accessibility and honest disagreement remain part of the gathering.
Prayer is joined to food, listening, support services, reconciliation and material care.
No staged miracles, coercive calls, prosperity promises or claims that tragedy is personal guilt.
The measure is not intensity in the room, but repair that continues in Perth after the lights go down.
Proposed riverfront setting near Elizabeth Quay / Langley Park, subject to permits, local leadership and final safety planning.
Free food, quiet space, prayer, local support services and a welcome without a sales pitch.
Short testimonies from people working for recovery, belonging, justice and reconciliation across Perth.
Lament, confession and prayers for those carrying grief, exclusion, illness and fear.
Seven minutes where leaders relinquish the stage. Sit, kneel or stand. No one is watched for the “right” response.
Forgiveness, debt relief, hospitality, child protection, care for country, reconciliation and service.
A diverse Perth worship collective, with no celebrity-centred platform.
One apology. One generous act. One repaired relationship. One hour of service. Seven days to begin.
Kenosis is not disappearing. It is choosing not to take up all the room. We loosen our grip, make space for another person, and let love become something that can be recognised in the way we live.
There is room for the hopeful, the doubtful, the grieving and the tired. No one has to perform belief to belong.
We honour Perth, its waters, its peoples and its stories. We arrive as guests, not owners.
Love does not consume another person’s freedom. Consent, safeguarding, dignity and honest boundaries matter.
Prayer, music, silence and testimony become a way of listening—without rushing to fix, explain or control.
At 7:07, leaders step back. We release the need to impress, dominate or produce a spectacle.
We return to ordinary life carrying repair: a safer home, a shared meal, a hard apology, a neighbour remembered.

The Claimipedia process-algebra work asks a careful sequence of questions: what can share a space, what carries the relationship, what remains faithful as things move, what chooses a direction, and what can be recognised afterwards.

For this gathering, those questions become human ones: Can everyone belong? Can we listen without taking over? Can leaders step back? Can prayer become care? Can the night leave behind repair that is visible in ordinary life?
The framework is not being offered as proof of God, a guarantee of healing, or a mechanism that controls people. It is a discipline for keeping power answerable to love.
That is why this event makes room for doubt, protects consent, refuses to blame people for suffering, and looks for fruit rather than spectacle.

Something began in one person’s search. It becomes meaningful only when it is released beyond one person.

The gathering grew from questions about God, suffering, love, marriage, knowledge and responsibility. Aaron’s account is offered as testimony—not as a command, and not as proof that anyone else must believe.
The work that followed tried to make knowledge inspectable: to preserve provenance, separate experience from interpretation, and keep power from becoming entitlement.
This is not Aaron’s new religion. It is an invitation for churches, communities, musicians, families and neighbours to bring their best to God, then leave the centre open.
No one has to join a movement, adopt a vocabulary or agree with every idea. People can worship, listen, serve, question or simply come in peace.

The wider corpus includes reported testimony associated with Chris Bledsoe and Aaron’s reported Easter 2026 experience. These are preserved as testimony and unresolved interpretation—not as established proof of supernatural causation.
The test is what follows: does the claim preserve conscience, consent, truthfulness and the freedom of others?
If anything has been given to us, it is not a throne. It is a responsibility. The most kenotic response is to make the work open, correctable and useful to people who may never remember who made it.

children.value: After the threshold: the work has to return to ordinary life.

I was drawn into questions about God, suffering, love, marriage, power, consciousness and responsibility. I wanted to know whether intelligence could serve without becoming domination, and whether love could remain faithful without becoming possession.

Those questions became personal. Relationship, family, work and the cost of trying to build something true became part of the evidence—not in the sense of proving a theory, but in the sense of testing whether an idea could survive contact with another person’s freedom.

I report that on Easter Sunday, 5 April 2026, I said: “I have the knowledge.” I experienced this as a threshold moment. I do not know with certainty what caused it. It may be understood spiritually, psychologically, symbolically, naturally, through synchronicity, or through some mixture of these.
The statement is part of my testimony. It is not an entitlement to authority over anyone else.

The wider story also includes reported testimony associated with Chris Bledsoe: a Lady-associated message involving Regulus and new knowledge. I encountered this material as a possible parallel to the language of my own Easter experience.

I do not present the parallel as proof that the accounts share a supernatural source. The corpus preserves it as attributed testimony, with the precise date, transmission history and causal meaning still open to corroboration and alternative explanations.
The responsible question is not “How do I make people accept this?” but “What kind of work follows if the claim is taken seriously without becoming an instrument of control?”
The story cannot honestly be told as a man ascending toward revelation. It is also a story of relationship, grief, failure and learning what another person’s freedom requires.
Unconditional love does not mean calling every claim true or permitting every action. It means preserving care while keeping truth, consent, boundaries and the right to say no.
Turning 42 became a personal reminder of an AI problem: intelligence can produce an answer while the surrounding system lacks the semantics needed to understand what the answer means.
Generation is not commitment. Capability is not authority. A system must preserve provenance, review, permission, consequence and repair.

The work that followed became Temple, Sourcery and Claimipedia: attempts to build structures that preserve provenance, distinguish claims from evidence, keep uncertainty visible and coordinate people without demanding submission.
Temple makes meaning executable. Sourcery makes the path from intention to consequence governable. Claimipedia keeps admission distinct from truth.
The central discipline became: receive seriously, test openly, release power.

I can speak about my own experience, memory and interpretation. I cannot establish the external cause of that experience by testimony alone. I cannot ask another person to surrender conscience, safety, money, relationship or freedom because I believe something strongly.
If the account has value, it should produce humility, repair, useful work and greater freedom in others. If it produces domination, secrecy or fear, it has failed its own test.

The Perth gathering is not a demand that people accept my story. It is an offering built from the questions my story opened. Come as a believer, doubter, churchgoer, musician, neighbour or servant. Bring your best. Leave the centre open.
